column121: I was practicing landings on Runway XX at ZZZ; the wind was variable at 3 kts. After five short field landings; I switched to soft field landings. On my second second soft field landing; the wind was at about 240 degrees (judging from the windsock); so I was correcting for a small crosswind from the left. I had a nice stable approach; a good transition; and a good soft touch down. I closed the carb heat; raised the flaps and throttled back up to take off. Immediately after throttling up I got a significant gust from the right which lifted my right wing; turned me to the left and lifted the plane back into the air. I was still correcting for a left crosswind; so this took me by surprise. I was able to catch it with right rudder and get the wings level; but by then I was off the runway to the left at about 30 degrees off the runway. Since the left wing came down suddenly (actually the right wing came up); I thought I blew a left tire. I was airborne at about 5'; but only going about 50 kts; so I wasn't climbing. In the moment; I didn't understand why the plane wasn't climbing (full throttle). I checked that the flaps were up and then decide to close the throttle and get the plane back on the ground. Once the wheels were on the ground; I was able to keep the nose up; but didn't want to stomp on the brakes or make any abrupt turns as I was in the dirt infield. As I got the plane slowed down; I was across the infield and approaching Runway XX. I was able to take a quick look left and saw that no one appeared to be on the runway heading my way.Once on Runway XX; I came harder on the brakes; but saw a taxiway light dead ahead. I diverted left enough to avoid a prop strike; but still hit the light with my right wheel. I stopped approximately thirty feet past the light off the south side of Runway XX. The tower called and asked if we were okay. I said that I thought I had blown a tire; but that I was fine. I also told him I had taken out the taxiway light. The tower instructed me to shut down and stay put; and that there were sending someone out.I shut down the engine and got out to inspect the plane. All the tires were fine and there didn't appear to be any damage to the plane. We rolled the plane back onto the runway. A mechanic arrived and suggested that we take the plane down to his shop to look it over. They couldn't tow the plane because it had wheel pants; so I taxied it to the shop.The mechanic looked the plane over and determined that a there was no damage except a small crack in the front of the right wheel pant where it hit the light. The prop was fine and didn't appear to even have any dirt on it. He provided a written statement that it could be returned to service and suggested I call the flying club to confirm the next steps. I called the owner of the plane and let him know that everything was okay except the wheel pant. I then called the VP of Operations for FBO and explained all of the above. They said that if the mechanic had cleared the plane; then I could fly back to ZZZ1 and meet with him and the plane owner.I taxied back to Runway XX and confirmed that the plane was handling normally on the ground. The wind was now 260 at 9kts but gusting to 16kts. I did a full run-up before departing. On initial roll-out; I paid close attention to the plane's reactions and was prepared to abort the take off if there were any abnormalities. The plane flew perfectly; So I returned to ZZZ1. I then met with the plane owner and VP of Operations to discuss what had happened. After discussing the landing; they had some suggestions for the future. They noted that ZZZ is notorious for having a significant wind shift from one end of the runway to the other. He suggested that if I had been quicker with full right rudder; I could probably have salvaged the take off. He suggested I work on being more active on the rudder on landing; especially in gusty conditions.After discussing the landing with my Instructor; he said Ishould be more patient with the landing phase of touch and goes (especially soft field landing ops) and to be sure the plane was completely settled (not flying anymore); and check to see that the flaps were fully retracted before throttling back up for takeoff. He also suggested that I switch to other training agenda (not landings) if it gets gusty.I believe that the unexpected gust from the right (when I was correcting for left crosswind) hitting me just as I throttled up (with the flaps probably still coming up) caused the plane to be lifted off at a low speed and put off course - something I could have caught if I had been better prepared/expecting it. I'm glad the plane wasn't damaged but also appreciate the important lesson regarding cross wind landings in gusty conditions. I've done well with cross wind landings; but the next time I notice it getting so gusty; I will simply call it a day until I have more cross wind experience.

column121: Installation of the RH Nose Landing Gear Door bumper on Aircraft X. After installing the bumper I went back to check that the bumper was secured to door stop. I moved the center control rod out several times checking the bumper security. After being informed on [date] that the aircraft had a returned flight due to the nose gear door problems; I am unsure at this time if the maintenance action I preformed was a factor in to the return to field event.This incident happened during the COVID-19 crisis. After being off for several weeks on a normal sleep routine. We were asked to return to work on a limited and staggered work schedule. I was off work approximately 8 weeks prior. This situation caused me to be off work and on a normal sleep schedule and then returning to work for one day on a night shift schedule. I could tell that I was fatigued due to the abnormal interruption of my circadian rhythm. The task I was performing has very limited instructions in the maintenance manual. I recommend a specific task be written to install just the rubber bumper on the nose gear door stop. These rubber bumpers frequently fall off and it is a common occurrence to replace them. I also noticed that the door stop on the nose landing gear doors can cause the nose gear door to appear open and locked when in fact the over-center linkage of the door is not in its locked position. This could potentially cause a sequence issue during door operation. This situation can be easily missed.

column121: I started my day by arriving at the airport [early] this morning. I got a cart out and hooked up the Chieftain to tow it to self serve it to get my fuel for the trip to ZZZ. I unpinned the nose gear linkage and towed it to the fuel farm; took the fuel I needed; then towed it back. It was raining pretty heavily by now and ceilings were reported overcast at 800 feet. After towing it back to the passenger pickup area I took the golf cart back to the hangar and put it away; then went back to the FBO to do final weather check; file flight plans; and load snacks and drinks. After giving gas enough time to settle I went out to the airplane to do the preflight. I did a walk around; sumped the fuel; checked the oil; but apparently missed putting the pin back in for the nose gear linkage. The passengers arrived on time and we departed within a few minutes of our targeted departure time. We broke out of the clouds at around 4;000 feet and had nice smooth flying for the whole 2.3 hrs down to ZZZ with a slight tailwind. The approach and landing were normal except for a bit after I had lowered the gear and verified three green I felt a slight 'clunk' and a stiffening of the rudder pedals like it usually does once the nose gear is down and locked. The abnormality was that I had already had a three green indication well before feeling that click. I verified three green again and everything felt normal at that point. Touchdown was smooth and I lowered the nose wheel slowly and then I started hearing a scrubbing noise. I immediately knew it what it was and pulled the yoke all the way back and held it there during slowdown without hitting the brakes. Fortunately I was close to my aft CG which I'm sure helped to keep the nose wheel off the ground a lot longer. As the tail lost lift the nose wheel touched the ground and started slowly pulling to the right side of the runway. I was almost completely stopped by the time the right main gear dropped off the small ledge of the pavement and onto the lower paved area of the runway lights. As soon as that happed the nose wheel stopped dragging and stopped pulling to the right. I let tower know we had an issue and asked for a tug and a ride for the passengers. When I deplaned I saw that the gear linkage pin was not installed and that the nose wheel had turned about 180 and was rolling smoothly again. After the passengers got off and were taken back to the FBO maintenance came out and we turned the wheel back around; installed the pin and hooked up a tug; then towed it to the maintenance hangar on the field.

column121: I took off at approximately XA:55 headed to ZZZ1. I planned on an XB:30 arrival in to ZZZ1 to request my IFR clearance. I arrived early and went into the FBO to pay any facility fees. My two friends arrived at around XB:45 and we were given a ride out the airplane on the golf cart. Copied down my IFR clearance and taxi instructions and received take off clearance at XC:10. I contacted Departure Control on a 090 heading while climbing to 2;000 feet and received clearance to climb to 4;000 feet. I then contacted a second departure frequency and was assigned a heading of 130 and final altitude of 8;000 feet instead of the 9;000 feet as filed. As of this point the flight was uneventful with clear skies and smooth ride. Nearing the top of climb I noticed that I lost JPI 700 (engine monitor). I took note of this and considered it an instrumentation issue and was not too concerned as I use the aircrafts primary engine gauges.Then; [I] lost the transponder and briefed my friends that we needed to land to check the transponder. I suspected an avionics malfunction and recycled the avionics switch with no luck. I also checked the circuit breakers; the ammeter and the annunciator lights; everything looked normal. I decided to divert as I started a right descending turn. I Then lost the Garmin 430 with the built in com1 radio just and I continued a descent and recycled the avionics switch once more; alternator switch and even master switch. I recycled the on off switch on the Garmin 430 with no luck and switched to com2 radios. The com2 radio was working but could only hear muffled replies from Approach. I also tried using co-pilots audio jacks just in case there was an issue with the jacks on the left. At that point I decided to go to ZZZ instead of ZZZ3 as I was familiar with the airport and knew the on field Maintenance personnel and would determine the avionics issue on the ground instead of continuing to problem shoot in the air. I overflew the field at 2000 feet to determine traffic in the pattern. I identified two Cessna 172's and a couple of Paramotors just west of the runway. My main priority became traffic avoidance due to the lack of radios.I made a teardrop 45 entry to left downwind and watched a C172 turning base and another on a climb out. I continued to slow down to gear extension speed and selected the gear down switch and felt the gear extend continued to slow to flap speed and selected first notch of flaps turned base and selected second notch of flaps and full flaps on final. Flew a normal approach and had no gear alarm and didn't suspect the gear to be up. I touched down with the gear up and realized what had happened as the airplane skidded down the runway and off to the right into the grass. This happened quickly and I don't quite recall the exact order of events but I do remember instructing my friends to exit the plane as I turned the fuel selector to off; turned off all the switches and removed the key. Verified that everybody was okay then prepared to deal with what just occurred. I have repeatedly ran this through my head since it happened and continue to think off how differently and simply I could've handled the situation. I feel like I went with the most obvious and easy option of trouble shooting on the ground and landing at a known uncontrolled field instead of reviewing all possible problems first. I mistakenly identified the initial problem as just an avionics failure; then a partial electrical failure but failed to identify a complete electrical failure until I skidded to a complete stop. I understand and have practiced emergency gear extensions and would've easily managed that if I suspected a gear issue. If the scenario were a stuck gear I would have attempted a forced gravity drop or the worst-case scenario an intentional gear up emergency landing after holding to burn off fuel. My biggest mistake was to not recognize all potential problems and identify the actual complete electrical failure.My recommendation and prevention of a similar incident Would be to approach any seemingly small issue as an indicator of a larger underlying problem and review all possible potential problems that may be associated with it. Also the most obvious solution may not be the best solution; take your time and aviate if an immediate landing is not required. Not all emergencies are initially presented as a major failure. A clear VFR day in close proximity of a known airport made it seem like the obvious and easy step to take would be to land and deal with the problem on the ground. I had plenty of fuel and did not feel stressed or rushed; my main focus or distraction became the other traffic in the pattern that I was unable to communicate with instead of the issues I had in my aircraft.

column121: During the initial take-off of a multi-engine training flight; the instructor retarded the mixture of the left engine to simulate an engine failure on takeoff.  As the flying pilot; I executed the first two steps of the published emergency procedure (1. Throttles to IDLE; 2. Apply maximum braking) upon aural recognition of the loss of power along with a significant (45-60 degree) yaw to the left. To counteract the left yaw; full right rudder and differential braking was applied. The aircraft responded to the control input and swerved back to approximate alignment with the runway; but by then had deviated far enough left that the left main tire was off the hard surface and into the grass.  The aircraft again yawed slightly to the left and the nose tire left the hard surface. Once the main and nose tires left the runway; additional control inputs to correct to the right were ineffective and the aircraft came to a stop in approximately 75 feet.  Attempts to return to the pavement from the resting position were ineffective and the aircraft was shut down. Upon exiting the aircraft; the nose wheel was determined to be buried nearly to the top of the tire in a muddy rut which was 30-40 feet long.  With the assistance of airport personnel and maintenance personnel from the flight school the aircraft was tipped back toward the tail far enough to raise the nose wheel out of the mud and put a 3X5 foot board under it to support its weight.  The aircraft was pulled back onto the runway and towed to the flight school using a standard tow bar.As for a root cause analysis of the events leading up to the incident; I think there are several:1. Relative inexperience of flying pilot: I had 5.9 hours in the aircraft and this was my third flight with this instructor.  Two previous flights occurred with a different instructor at a different school; the most recent being 35 days prior to this incident.  I had to switch schools as the aircraft at the original training site became unavailable due to long-term maintenance issues.  This was my second-ever engine failure on takeoff practice.  The maneuver was not briefed by the instructor; though I assumed it was likely to occur.2. Slow reaction time: I noticed the change in engine noise just prior to the onset of adverse yaw.  I believe I hesitated for a second or less prior to pulling the throttles to idle.  This exacerbated the yaw which ultimately led to the runway departure.3. Misunderstanding of the written emergency procedure: I applied significant braking as I attempted to control the aircraft and prevent it from exiting the runway; to include differentially applying heavier braking to the right main.  During a debrief with the instructor and flight school owner; they explained that the heavy braking may have reduced directional control of the aircraft.  I saw no evidence of locked brakes; but I am not an expert in such matters.  As a low time multi-engine pilot; I suppose I have to defer to the instructors' experience. Given the discussion surrounding the potential negative impact of applying maximum braking during this procedure it seems that the phrase 'Braking-As Required' or similar might be better than 'Braking-Maximum' as written in the flight school's current checklist.4. Failure of the instructor to back me up on the controls on only my second exposure to this maneuver.  As mentioned; I may have hesitated briefly before retarding the throttles to idle. It was suggested that this may have allowed the situation to develop into and unrecoverable maneuver; but at no point did the instructor physically touch either throttle or verbally indicate I needed to take different actions.
column123: While doing a multi engine training flight there was a loss of directional control on the runway. When performing a takeoff; the engine failure on takeoff maneuver was being performed. The mixture to the left engine was closed to simulate an engine failure shortly after applying power for takeoff. There was a momentary pause by the student ~ 2 seconds before the throttles were closed. As the throttles were closed the nose of the aircraft was pointed roughly 45' to the left side of the runway. While trying to regain control of the aircraft; the student at the controls applied max brakes to get the aircraft to stop. With the aircraft pointed towards the side of the runway; and max force being applied to the brakes; little usable rudder force was left for the instructor's rudder pedals. The nose was slowly pulled to the right; but the momentum of the aircraft caused the plane to come off the runway. The left main gear and nose gear were off the side of the runway in the grass with the right main still on the runway. Within the past 24 hours there had been substantial rainfall at the airport. The turf next the runway was wet and waterlogged. When the nose gear of the aircraft left the pavement; it caused the nose to sink into the grass ~ 12-14 inches. With the reduced clearance of the nose gear; and the right engine still over the runway; the blade of the right engine struck the pavement. After coming to a complete stop both engines were shut down and the aircraft wasn't moved until maintenance inspected the aircraft. After reflecting on the events that lead to this occurrence there a few lessons I have learned. First is having a more open communication with the student about what is expected of them during the recovery of a maneuver such as a single engine failure on takeoff. A more thorough brief should be discussed on what the corrective action looks like during this maneuver and what does directional control mean on the runway. A demonstration of the correct recovery done by the instructor might also be performed so a clear standard is set.

Upon review/discussion of the situation with my flight instructor a couple hours after the incident we concluded the following items could have potentially contributed to the runway excursion:- Potential excessive speed in the round out leading to either bouncing/floating or the nose coming off the ground and the airplane weather vaning into the wind without appropriate left rudder being applied as needed. - Potentially removing crosswind correction (left rudder) upon landing- Potentially did not apply additionally needed left rudder crosswind correction due to a gusting windPotential Learning Points: - The ATIS reported crosswinds were below what had been previously practiced; but crosswinds had not been specifically practiced in almost 5 months. - Request winds from Tower in case they have changed from ATIS reported winds.- Anticipate the need to continue flying the airplane after touchdown.

I then came to a stop and shut down the engine. After shutting; I addressed the passengers and then exited the aircraft to inspect the damage. He also said he attempted to stop the aircraft by grabbing it with his arm; resulting in a bruise on his left forearm. The single lineman was not directly in front of our aircraft; but standing just to the right; directly behind the tail of the Caravan. He didn't give the typical 'move forward' motion with his arms; just a thumbs up to indicate we were good to start moving. I released the brake and began moving forward a few feet; before turning to right towards the taxiway and the gap between the aircraft. The First Officer was focused on the right wing; announcing a 'clear right'. As my left wing approached the Caravan; the lineman gave thumbs up indicating we were clear of the other aircraft; so I announced 'clear left'. I looked forward and briefly looked to the right to assess the distance. As I looked back to the left; from my perspective it looked clear; but a little close; so I attempted to slow down and turn to the right. This is when I was given a stop signal; but as I began applying the brakes is when the wing made contact with tail of the Caravan. [I] suggest more wing walkers when taxiing out of the overflow area in ZZZ.

When I got out of the aircraft I noticed that the flaps were stuck at 20 degrees (even though the flap lever had been all the way up) and that the propeller had been chipped up at the ends. column121: The flight was conducted on date in Aircraft X. The flight was filed IFR (in VMC conditions) from ZZZ to ZZZ1. The aircraft was fresh out of 50 hour inspection. On board was myself in the left pilot's seat weighing; and two passengers weighing 180 lbs; the other passenger weighing 220 lbs. Weight and balance configuration computed this was a safe configuration with the 1000 lbs of fuel onboard.The flight was relatively normal between ZZZ and ZZZ1 with the exception of hitting moderate turbulence for approximately 2 min just outside of ZZZ1.Descent into ZZZ1 was normal; and everything about setting up for the visual approach was on track as it should have been. After turning base to final; a normal glidepath was established; and the aircraft slowed to the landing flap configuration speed of 112 kts.; and the landing flaps were selected. A normal glidepath was set aiming at the runway numbers. The aircraft needed approximately 3 degrees of left wing down; and a slight amount of right rudder due to the winds being reported as 220 at 8 kts. The final landing configuration was again checked; and the aircraft was landed approximately 600 ft. down the runway approximately 3 - 4 ft. left of centerline. The aircraft made a small bid to the left; and the crosswind controls were relaxed slightly to track the nose down centerline. The nose gear was lowered to the runway as the rudder crosswind correction was shifted to neutral. As the nose gear touched the runway surface the aircraft started a hard-right steer toward the right runway edge. Left rudder and left brake were applied; but the airplane did not correct back to the left. As the airplane continued toward the right side of the runway; more left rudder and left brake was applied; as well as right brake to try to slow the aircraft overall. The aircraft did not respond to any rudder/nosewheel steering inputs and departed the paved surface on the right side; skidding through the unprepared grass area.The aircraft came to a complete stop by high-siding and hitting the left wingtip in the dirt; as well as the propeller. The engine was shutdown using the condition lever; and by pulling the emergency fuel cutoff lever. The battery switch was turned off; and the aft passenger opened the door and both passengers evacuated the aircraft; while I stayed behind to secure the cockpit. No fuel leaks were noted.Once the aircraft interior was secure; I exited the aircraft and waited for airport emergency vehicles to arrive. Inspection of the aircraft post-accident showed damage to the left outboard wing; the left main gear strut; the propeller; and a skin wrinkle just forward of the aircraft door. Review of the aircraft path on the runway and through the grass showed no damage to the runway; runway lights; or any runway markings.My research after the runway excursion has revealed that the PA-46 series of aircraft has a long history of this type of scenario and runway excursions. Most have happened to the PA-46-500TP version; and were attributed to a nose gear/motor mount design that Piper put out a series of advance directives to fix. While I am still investigating; I have found 5 total of the new M600 that have had runway excursions. My opinion is that the nose gear design is flawed and in some instances; does not fully rotate into position as it extends. Thus causing the nose wheel to be cocked to one side. Upon contact with the runway; the nose gear goes into a caster; thus forcing the aircraft to travel in the direction of the nose gear. There are too many of these incidents and the design needs scrutiny and needs to be changed.

column121: The aircraft was returned to the parking stand following a report by ground crew that; immediately following engine start; the right engine fan blades were emitting sparks covering the entire inner shroud of the engine. A call was immediately placed to Dispatch; in which the CA (Captain) requested Maintenance be patched in via 3-way call so the engine issues could be conveyed directly to Maintenance Control. Following this call; both flight crew members went downstairs to inspect the engine and discuss the occurrence with Maintenance.The local Mechanic climbed into the engine cowl and shined a flashlight around the blades for less than a minute; before climbing down and stating the engine looked fine. The Mechanic then called Maintenance Control; who stated the engine needed a maintenance run-up. The Mechanic stated he was not qualified for run-ups. The Captain declined to do a maintenance run-up on the engine; as it appeared to have some type of mechanical failure; and the risk to both the engine and nearby personnel seemed excessive given such a cursory inspection by the Mechanic. Flight crew returned to the flight deck at this point.Within a few minutes; the Mechanic returned to the flight deck with a signed-off logbook stating the aircraft was 'good to go'. Without a qualified mechanic to complete a run-up available; Maintenance Control had authorized the Return To Service of the aircraft not having identified the source of the sparks. Determining that the return of the aircraft to service without understanding the defects in the engine was an unsafe action; and following a joint call with the Duty Pilot; Chief Pilot; and Dispatch; the Captain refused the aircraft.Shortly thereafter; the local Mechanic showed up with a rolled up piece of paper in his hands and said he had received 'emergency authorization for maintenance run-up'. Questioning this; the Captain requested to see the form. The Mechanic showed him a completely blank form with no Supervisor sign-off. When asked where his authorization was; the Mechanic said he 'could sign himself off'.The Captain told the Mechanic he would need to call the Company and verify. The Captain called Maintenance Control and explained the situation. Maintenance Control stated the Mechanic was qualified until year for engine runs; and that they hadn't realized it earlier. At this point; the mechanic climbed into the left seat of the flight deck and attempted 9 starts on the right engine. Not one start was successful; making it obvious to both the flight crew and the ground personnel that the Mechanic didn't even know how to start an engine on the 767.A cursory look into an engine with a flashlight is insufficient; given the report that an engine shroud was covered in sparks around the fan blades upon startup. Additionally; the aircraft had a recent maintenance history of bent fan blades. Serious issues like potential engine structural damage should result in a thorough inspection. It is very concerning that Maintenance Control requested an engine run-up to verify operational soundness; and then when the inspection could not be safely completed; attempts to sign off the aircraft as airworthy without the run-up. As far as the Mechanic goes; he himself originally stated he was 'not qualified for engine runs'. Just because he may have completed some training in the past; does not mean he was competent to start; and run-up an engine.

On downwind; I executed the landing checklist and made a normal landing.I believe the distraction of two traffic alerts resulted in both the student and me failing to complete the landing checklist. column121: Upon landing; my student and I had a propeller strike on the runway surface. With winds at 360 gusting up to 17 kts; we had a healthy crosswind. My student was handling the wind conditions well and made proper control inputs throughout the landing. Upon landing; the aircraft entered an extremely nose-low attitude which caused the propeller to strike the runway surface. As the plane began to enter its nose-low attitude; I realized that my student was not handling the after-landing process as I had anticipated. I immediately reached for the controls to make prompt corrective inputs and recover the aircraft into a normal after-landing attitude.Focusing on recovering the nose-low attitude and trying to bring the aircraft back into a safe position was all that occupied my mind at the moment. I failed to say 'My Controls' to my student which I believe; in turn; caused the student to remain on the controls and brakes while I attempted to recover the aircraft. With both of us on the controls; the aircraft was not responding properly to either of our inputs. The aircraft continued to travel to the right of centerline and exited the paved surface of the runway approximately 10-15 ft. where we brought it to a stop.As the CFI (Flight Instructor); my largest takeaway is in the area of communication with my student. Because of my immediate reaction to the situation; I did not communicate to him my intent to take control of the aircraft. I did not tell him to get his hands and feet off the controls. I did not make sure that he knew without doubt that I needed him off of his controls so I could have effective use of mine.My action moving forward with students will be specifically focused on effective communication and making sure there are no barriers between the message I send them; then confirming that they received that same message. Emphasizing the fact that if I say 'my controls' at any point during flight or ground operations; I need them to be 100% off of all the flight controls so I can have immediate and full effective use of my flight controls.During all phases of flight I will be taking specific action to verify and assure safety of flight so my student is briefed on what is to come as well as for my knowledge that the student understands what I am communicating to them. Another practice I will be revisiting with my students will be demonstrating safety risk management as a normal part of the landing and after-landing phases of flight.

column121: This jet had a recent history of engine bleed work and complaints of very loud cabin pack noise. Shortly after takeoff we received an ECAM Advisory for a #2 engine high Nacelle Temperature (250 C/ 482F). We were being vectored around thunderstorms in the departure area and took a radar vector north and a continued climb clearance. We swapped controls and I reviewed the applicable QRH supplementary section. We turned the #2 bleed off and that had no effect. We went to manual throttles and reduced power but that did not have a significant effect on the abnormally high temperature. As we climbed to FL 290 the ambient temperature dropped and the nacelle temp dropped but only slightly. It got to 215 C at the lowest point but that was still well above the 100 C of the number one engine and was still a flashing monitor. We continued the climb to see if the advisory would go away in cruise. We contacted Ground Operations on VHF and requested some Maintenance Control input into our decision making process. When we leveled off at FL 290 about 80 miles north of ZZZ; the advisory continued and nacelle temp began to climb again. Maintenance and Dispatch could not provide us any relevant information or recommendations. The QRH directs the crew to consider shutting down the motor if there are secondary indications. There was none.Based on this information; I thought that we had significant bleed air leak that I could not control with the engine bleed valve or thrust and that may lead to a fire or engine damage if we continued to proceed. I asked myself how would Company Training; Company Ops and the FAA view my judgement six months from now by overflying several good airports with a known engine problem just to bring ZZZ1 a broken jet (does ZZZ1 have power plant support?).We decided to turn back to ZZZ and landed. We did not request priority handling; no fuel was dumped. We did not land over max landing gross weight and no hazmat issue. I give myself a solid B for my performance and an A for my FO. We sat in a hot jet for over an hour since we have lost confidence in the data from auto verify information and felt that sitting in a hot jet is safer than hanging out together in the crew room (Covid petri dish). Running the APU in the Airbus without the landing gear doors down often results in a bleed leak that requires further maintenance. The quality of this risk management decision should not be viewed by the outcome but by the relevant facts that I had perceived at the time.

Then I shut off the fuel selector and magnetos and egressed the plane to head towards the FBO. The aircraft was put back on its wheels and towed to a hangar by airport management. The radios performed acceptably throughout the flight; but multiple occasions of extended downtime caused by mechanical needs over the last several months of ownership made staying proficient difficult. column121: On a cross country from ZZZ to ZZZ1; we did 3 touch and goes at ZZZ1 and then headed back to north to ZZZ. We climbed to cruise at 8500 ft. MSL and then upon reaching our TOD we went through our descent checklist. Then; descending through 6000 ft. MSL; my student added power to slow the descent and to level off. Immediately we had engine roughness; then a rise in RPMs then another drop in RPMs. I took controls and my student read our QRC for engine problems in flight. We slowed to our VG of 73 KIAS; made sure that the fuel shut off valve was open; enriched the mixture and had the same roughness; and then rise in rpms then a drop. We double checked that the fuel pump was on; we opened the alternate air and at about this time we had low rpms and the engine almost died. Then; we turned on the boost; prime; pump and got the last rise in RPMs and then the engine stopped producing power. The propeller was windmilling from aerodynamic force. At this time we were descending through 5700 ft. and did not check the mags as we did not feel that we had enough time to do so. We followed my [forced landing] training of ABCDE. A. airspeed; get to VG (73). B. Best place to land. My student and I discussed our glide ratio and determined that we did not have enough altitude to make it to the airport; and chose a field to land in and began setting up for landing. C. Checklist we began to go through our [forced] landing checklist; D. Declare; I [requested priority handling] Aircraft X is going down in a field east of a certain highway. About this time our propeller ceased spinning. E. Execute. We completed our [forced landing] checklist items and performed a soft field landing; touching down at 55 KIAS or slower. We rolled with our nose wheel off the ground for approximately 20 paces. at approximately 260 paces from touchdown the plane rolled into a slight depression of about 2 feet down and 4 feet 6 feet wide; and rolled up the other side of the depression on an equal rise of about 2 feet at which time the front nose wheel broke from the gear and the remaining NLG strut dug into the dirt and brought us to an abrupt stop causing the plane to pitch forward onto the nose at which time the propeller spinner was slightly dented on the bottom side. The pitching motion was not enough to make us flip tail over nose and we settled back down on the main landing gear and then rolled back down into the depression. Both my student and I were wearing seat belts and shoulder restraints and were unharmed. We secured the plane and then exited the aircraft and called for assistance. We both had prepared our cross country flight plans and our estimations for our fuel burn for our flight was between 9-10 gallons. Our preflight inspection showed our dipstick with just about 12 gallons and we had our school's dispatcher add 5 gallons which would give us a comfortable safety buffer. Yet upon landing and securing the plane we stuck the plane again and found it dry. This plane is known to have its fuel gauge read 6 gallons low on the gauge; and was showing near empty; which normally means that it should've had 6 gallons left based on previous experience.
column123: We took off from ZZZ to ZZZ1 back to ZZZ. Before the flight we checked the fuel and we had 12 gallons; on our flight plan it said that we would need approximately 8.9 gallons for the way there and back. We had our dispatcher go out to the plane and put in an extra 5 gallons; and when we visually check the tanks with the stick; it read right under 18 gallons; so probably around 17 gallons. The flight there was fine; the flight back was also ok until our descent. Before our descent we noticed that the fuel tank read 0. In a previous flight our tank read 0; but when we landed we visually checked the tank with the stick and it read 6 gallons. Coming out of decent at 6000 ft. MSL I went and put power back it. The RPMs came up as normal; then started sputtering. Immediately my instructor took controls. We enriched the mixed; cycled the throttle; and turned on the fuel prime. The engine was not going to get us there. He got the plane to our glide speed; 73 KIAS; as we quickly started doing math for whether or not we could make it to the airport to land. After some quick calculations we determined that we couldn't make it back; and we were going to have to find a field. After choosing our best place to land; we started going through [forced landing] checklists. At about 500 ft. AGL my instructor got on the radio and [advised ATC]. I then flipped to the [forced] landing checklist; ran through the steps; and then we executed the landing. We did a soft field landing keeping the nose up as long as we could; then rolled it out. All was fine until we saw a berm in the distance coming up fast. We hit the berm and the plane went up on the nose; then came right back down. We were at a complete stop; so I unbuckled quickly; opened the canopy; and back away from the plane; in fear that a fire may start. We both walked away from the accident ok. No injuries; we were wearing our seat belts; and were fine. Soon after the landing passerby's came to check on us; then 15 minutes later [medical and other officials] came to see what had happened.We made several flight plans on how much fuel should have been consumed; and kept coming to numbers around 9-10 gallons; and in the absolute worst conditions 14 gallons. Our 18 gallon load should have been plenty for us; but when we landed I visually checked the fuel with the stick; and we were completely empty.

column121: [I was] PIC flying pilot. Requested vectors for the RNAV 28 approach in VMC conditions. Wind variable 3 kts. Turned on outside the final approach fix. Aircraft was configured and stabilized at FAF and checklist completed. Descended via VNAV to 100 ft. above MDA then transitioned to VASI at this time. Transition from VNAV to VASI was briefed prior and confirmed at transition. Autopilot and yaw damp were disconnected between FAF and transition. Crossing the threshold; we discovered that the landing lights were not on. As we touched down normally I called for landing lights and momentarily looked up and to right to confirm switch position. At this time; the aircraft drifted left and a slight impact was felt by both crew. Aircraft was returned to the runway centerline. Post flight revealed damage to the left trailing flap and left leading edge due to impact with runway edge lights. I believe the primary reason for the lateral deviation was me as flying pilot removing complete attention to the lateral path of the aircraft at such a critical moment of the flight. Although I only diverted my eyes for a second it was enough time to become disoriented enough to allow the aircraft to drift left during a dark night landing. Had I simply concentrated on the left and right runway edge lights in front of me the roll out would have been dark but normal. It is possible-but not common-for the landing lights to extend but not sequence on. This is a situation neither the SIC or me had seen before. I believe modifying the SOP call to 'landing lights extend/on' instead of the checklist response of 'as required' could help alleviate confusion for future crews.

It was clear from the initial job assignments that these cards are taken very lightly and are considered nuisance cards or at least that is how they appeared. Aircraft X was assigned a XI:10 am trip and Aircraft Y was assigned a XG:30 am trip. The assignments were issued between XI:30 and XJ:00 pm. I myself have not entered an 'Entry to Park' AC and had many questions about the process as these airplanes were already at or beyond 48 hrs. on the ground. We were told to place Aircraft X into parking and leave it and to park and return to service Aircraft Y. This created much confusion for us on Aircraft Y. How do you park and return to service an aircraft immediately? Why are these cards issued now? Why the lack of manpower? What did they expect from us? How do we even accomplish these task in such a short amount of time? Do we have the ability to [apply] N/A to boxes? How did these surpass the clock? If we have to drain the water system and deactivate the heaters where are the planes parked to refill and reactivate? What equipment is available to get up to the tail and how far to get it there? Is there garbage on the airplane and do we have to dump it as per the card? Do we have to cover the pitot [tubes] only to take the tape off immediately? What airplane is the priority; the early out (because different parking spots indicate different abilities)? Why did safe go into maintenance mode when we were reviewing safe? Why did our ability to print the Procedures Manual go out for a half hour? Who do we contact; as the card suggested? Because management didn't have the answers for the questions we asked; I made two attempts to call Tech Services and the company phone dropped off and I had to use my cell and then that dropped off. The clock was ticking we made a choice to start with the aircraft on the gate after we found its location because it was going into parking and staying for dayshift. This gave us time for people to come back with the answers we needed to know about putting an aircraft into parking and taking it out immediately and how to handle. Normally we would have started with the early out aircraft. Mechanic A felt the pressure with comments such as they are going to expect these airplanes. My reassurance to him 'don't worry we just do our best' wasn't enough and he made a stand move alone while myself and Mechanic B were in the cabin and hit Aircraft X taking that airplane out of service with a 2.5 by 2.75 dent on the frame. The team was disheartened to say the least and we notified management immediately. After they arrived; Mechanic A was very distraught. I let them know that we did not even get to Aircraft Y yet and asked if they have an answer and what was the expectation for that plane. The answer was no answer yet; and yes they still expect that plane. This was around XA:30 to XB:00 am. So with that we finished off Aircraft X and the entry to park then we went to lunch very late; way past our union contract time. When I got back from lunch; all the paper work I had printed to start the next aircraft was removed from the east office and in some type of transportation mode so all the work was missing. Looking for the work brought us around XD:30 am and still could not locate it. End of shift was XE:30 and so we abandoned any potential work to be done on Aircraft Y. What is their expectations to accomplish an Entry to Parking and a Return to Service in a single night just for the sake of accomplishment with no real positive outcome other than to risk a failure?The cards need to be made more realistic or the company needs to be more realistic about their flight schedulesand actual workload. This whole program of parking needs to be revamped. This whole process left more questions than answers and different interpretations. It's a real mess in my personal opinion and in some cases may lead mechanic who has a work efficiency outlook to do it way different (some would say cut corners) than a mechanic who has a processes outlook and will park the plane before lunch then would return to service after lunch wasting materials and supplies and filling landfills simply because they realize that is the process.
column123: I was assigned to work 2 airplanes Aircraft X required an Entry to Park and Aircraft Y required Entry to Park and required to Return to Service. We didn't receive any direction and it didn't seem to make sense but we tried to comply as the best we could. I know they wanted the airplanes in the morning but I didn't see how we can do it without taking some shortcuts. Their expectations seemed high. We did our best. Many times if I ask for help it creates more problems so I try to be independent. As I was pushing a stand; there was an air conditioning hose in the way and I turned off the power and flattened the hose. I probably should have disconnected it; now that I look back; but at the time I have done this before as I observed other mechanics do and as I went over the hose I fell the stand got away from me because of the weight and it hit the plan. column121: While en route from ZZZ to ZZZ1 the engine of Aircraft X abruptly quit with no warning. At that point I established best glide speed; shut off my fuel selector; and landed it in a clearing in the forest with no bodily harm; no damage to other people or property; and some aircraft damage. Before flight this morning I looked into the fuel tanks and noted around 1/3 in both tanks; topped off the fuel with 72 gallons over the top of the wing; and visually double checked that the fuel was full after allowing for equalization then departed ZZZ at approximately XA00 am. The engine quit between 1:35- 1:40 into the flight. The left tank fuel gauge appeared to be inoperative when I departed but since I was not familiar with the airplane I did not know if it had been disabled or if it would come back into service throughout the flight (it has been my experience that they do some times). The right fuel gauge seemed a little erratic but was counting down the fuel as I progressed throughout the flight. When the engine quit the right tank gauge was not indicating empty. I chose that the airplane was safe for this flight concerning the fuel because of my conservative fuel planning process that I have used successfully on many other ferry flights with different aircraft. I talked to several pilots with 1340 experience and it sounded like the most I could expect it to burn would be around 36 gph using the power settings that I intended to use. I made my flight plan to ZZZ1 assuming 40 gph and decided I would divert to a closer airport if I could not make it there in less than 2 hours; leaving me with 40 minutes of reserve. I would have made it at about 1:45. After the fact; I calculated my actual fuel burn using the 106 gallons usable that was placarded on the wing and came up that the engine was burning 62 gph. This seems extraordinarily high and I am suspicious that the engine quit for a different reason or that fuel was being leaked in flight. In hindsight I can see that only flying a 1 hour leg first with an unfamiliar airplane would be best practice that I will employ from now on now that I understand how far off fuel consumption estimates can be. I also will insist that the fuel gauges be functioning to the best of their designed ability as a secondary monitoring system in any aircraft that I fly.

column121: After leveling off for cruise. I pulled the power levers to set cruise power. The plane was losing airspeed rapidly so I request a descent. The propeller was wobbling in the air stream and the plane was shaking. Loss of power [occurred] right away. At the time I had no idea [why]. column121: Pilot and a singe passenger were returning for a landing in VMC (winds light and variable); and cleared For landing by Tower. After what appeared to be a normal landing; on-centerline and during roll-out;(the plane was rolling below 30 kts); the aircraft unexpectedly began to pull to the right. The pilot attempted to correct using left rudder pressure and toe brake. The combination of left rudder pressure and left toe brake did not appear to exert sufficient braking authority or correct the turn. The aircraft seemed very slow to correct direction. The pilot continued with left rudder pressure and applied the handbrake. The plane immediately slowed; but rolled off the right side of the marked runway (and onto the apron) as the pilot was able to regain directional control. This was just past the first taxiway; where the underside of the right wing scraped the top edge of the taxiway sign. There did not appear to be any damage to the sign; but the bottom skin of the right wing was later found to be torn; in a line perpendicular to the leading edge; on the outboard side of the wing; about half-way to the from the front of the wing; and the skin tear exposed the bottom edge of the wing spar; which appeared to be nicked. Using the handbrake only from that point on; the pilot was able to return to the runway centerline and taxi the plane on the runway to the next taxiway and then navigate to parking with no further directional control problems. The incident was promptly reported and the plane was grounded for inspection and repair at visual inspection by a qualified A&P.It had been noted that on one prior flight that the plane had unexpectedly pulled to the right; but that the problem had been evaluated and resolved. On pre-flight taxi and takeoff during the flight on which the incident occurred; the plane did not appear to be pulling excessively to the right; so the pilot believed that the earlier squawk had been resolved; and the pilot decided to conduct the flight as planned. The pilot was well-rested; in good health; and alert during the flight. A potential distractor was that the oil access door on the cowling popped open on climb-out after takeoff (this resulted in the decision to return to land and correct the issue before continuing the flight). It is possible that this issue may have distracted the pilot. Also; the pilot may not have reacted quickly enough when the plane began pulling to the right on roll-out; and may not have transitioned quickly enough from applying the toe brake (which did not appear to be effective)to using the handbrake (which applied effective braking on both mains). Finally; as a final possible preventive action; the pilot might have elected to touch-down on the left side of the wide runway; anticipating the possibility of the plane pulling to the right.

column121: While conducting a Flight Review; my client pilot was practicing a power-off 180-degree approach to landing (simulated emergency) when we encountered wind shear. The winds were approximately 13 gusting 18 knots from 210 and the aircraft was on a modified left base while angling toward Runway XX at ZZZ. The descent path was normal for a glide to the beginning of the runway and airspeed was approximately 85 KT. At about 1;000 feet from the runway and 300 feet AGL; the pilot lowered the landing gear while passing into the lee of a dense woodlot that stands about 600 feet south and west of the extended runway centerline; and there we experienced a sudden and dramatic loss of airspeed; down to approximately 65 knots. (Of course; some loss of airspeed was expected as the gear deployed.) I called for power as the aircraft began to pitch down and descend. (The Pilot Flying was guarding the throttle.) I continued to shout for more power over the next 2-3 seconds as the aircraft descended to perhaps 15 feet AGL; still 500 feet short of the runway.I took control of the airplane as the pilot brought in full power. We were now grazing the tops of the corn in the field below us and I could see a 15' fence coming up quickly. I felt we had very little angle of attack available - perhaps just enough to climb 10' to clear the fence. I increased elevator as much as I dared; then lowered the nose again once past the fence. Because of our low airspeed and high angle of attack; though the propeller cleared the fence; the top of a fence post contacted and tore the skin of the airplane's belly just aft of the gear legs. As airspeed slowly recovered; I climbed to perhaps 20 feet AGL; then reduced power as we reached the runway and made a normal landing. I have been flying for more than XX years and I have never experienced such a dramatic loss of airspeed. My corrective action to prevent a similar crisis will include the following.1. I will not use the actual beginning of runways to practice power-off landings; but instead have clients treat the touch down zone (1;000 feet down the runway) as their landing target.2. I will be more prepared to push; move; or overpower client pilots if they do not immediately respond to verbal instructions. 3. I will be more mindful of the potential for wind shear; especially when operating downwind of significant obstacles (the wood lot; in this case) on windy days.

column121: During a flight to maintain currency an upset event occurred.  Aircraft X took off from ZZZ on a VFR flight with flight following.  After takeoff and communication hand off from ZZZ Tower to Departure; Aircraft X was instructed by ATC to maintain runway heading due to traffic.  After watching the traffic pass on the moving map display and no other traffic in the immediate area; asked ATC for permission to proceed on course.  ATC apologized for the delay and cleared Aircraft X to proceed on course.  Leveling off at 5;500 feet MSL and after visually and electronically checking for traffic; setup for slow flight and approach to stall practice.  Retarded throttle; airspeed was already below 165 knots so landing gear was extended; verified all gear was down and locked.  Held altitude while speed bleed off; applying flaps incrementally until fully extended.  Began stabilized slow flight; adjusting throttle and pitch as necessary to maintain 5;500 feet.  Winds at 5;500 MSL were 18 knots and there was some light turbulence.  After 1-2 minutes of steady slow flight the airspeed indicator dropped quickly even though there were no rapid throttle or control surface adjustments.  The stall horn began sounding continuously and the aircraft experienced very slight buffeting at which point full throttle and downward pitch were applied simultaneously and in the same instant the right wing dropped extremely rapidly as if the aircraft had been commanded into a snap roll.  The roll continued even as left aileron and left rudder were applied with no effect and in less than 2 seconds the aircraft was inverted.  At this point the nose dropped and the aircraft entered a right-hand spiral dive.  The throttle was immediately retarded and standard recovery efforts begun.  Attempts to level the wings were complicated by the g-forces as the pilot struggle to remain upright.  At least 5-7 right hand turns occurred in spite of left aileron input.  At approximately 500-700 feet AGL; control was reestablished and the aircraft returned to zero roll.  A climb was initiated and as the airspeed dropped the pilot remembered the aircraft was still in full landing configuration with the throttle at idle.  Power was added; flaps retracted one notch and the landing gear was retracted.  Continued retracting flaps one notch at a time as speed and altitude increased.After returning to a safer altitude; all aircraft controls were checked and seemed to be normal with no apparent explanation for the un-commanded roll.  Only after landing and examining the aircraft was the extreme damage noted.  Apparently during the spiral dive; the aircraft exceeded speed and g-force limitations even though the pilot does not recall an overspeed warning.

column121: Normal day; normal passenger operations; on Aircraft X; performing ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight. With APU being under MEL; started engine number one at the gate according to normal checklist. Cleared to push out of the gate; to the blue line. The initial push back was mostly smooth. Aircraft pushed on a slant angle on the green line and stopped. Tow truck driver contacted the flight deck; stating that he will pull us to the blue line. Since then; the mild tensions and sounds were sensible as if it felt that the angle of pulling forward to the blue line was kind of steep. I; personally; could not see the tow truck from the right seat. Shortly after; we heard a bigger noise and aircraft started to move forward that followed immediately by the driver asking us to set the brake in a rushed voice; Captain acted promptly; and we stopped the aircraft on time and smoothly. I personally did not feel any impact. We stopped with an angle on the blue line. The driver mentioned that the tow bar broke and he is going to disconnect and contact the ramp safety. We communicated with the Ramp; Operations and MX (Maintenance) Control. Captain communicated with the flight attendants and made an announcement to the passengers informing them about the nature of problem. Within 10 minutes or so; with the supervision of our MX personnel on the ground; a new tow truck; new tow bar and a new driver towed us back to the same gate. This time it was very smooth. We found out that a scratch line and a shallow dent exist on the lower right-hand side of the aircraft. It happened by the shallow impact of the fuselage with the roof of the tow truck. Captain wrote up the damage in MX logbook. Dispatch and Flight Operations have been informed. Everybody acted professional during and after the event. Don't know if the tow bar breaking happened because of the angle & the tension exposed to it; or it was the material failure. Tail swap happened shortly after; and we performed the same flight on ship (tail). If a tow truck driver is not happy with the location of the aircraft or if for some reason they are in a tight spot; or any other unusual issue; they can always consider us as a team and communicate any unease with us; so we all figure out how to get out of it. My assumption is that if we were unhooked from the tow bar on the green line; the entire event could have been avoided. It could only cost me a simple radio call to the ramp; I guess.
column123: These are my recollections as I remember them: We were operating Aircraft X operating out of gate X. Aircraft X was operating with MEL APU Inoperative applied. We complied with procedures for engine start with external pneumatic air source & completed the appropriate normal checklists. Ramp tower assigned us a push back onto the blue line. The push back seemed normal with the exception that the AC (aircraft) was at an odd angle. I attributed this to the push crew having to avoid the construction adjacent to N11. The tug driver announced that he would get us over to the blue line & proceeded to turn the jet that direction. At this point I could sense some stress on the tug/towbar combination but nothing that seemed abnormal. As the driver proceeded towards the blue line the noise the towbar was making got louder until we heard what I'd describe as a pop or snap. At this point the jet rolled forward due to forward momentum & the driver or wing walker said set the brakes. I estimate the jet moved forward about 10 feet as I was applying the brakes. We verified that there were no injuries to any of the push back crew & were informed that everyone on the ramp was safe. I stopped the jet as judicially as I could; taking into account that the FA's (flight attendants) were probably standing; conducting their safety demonstration. The driver announced he needed to have the Ramp Safety Supervisor conduct an inspection & we called Line Maintenance to survey the situation. We called the cabin to verify there were no injuries to guests or crew & subsequently a PA was made by me to inform the guests of our situation. Line Maintenance asked us if we could taxi the jet back to gate under power which I declined; not knowing the extent of any possible damage. A new towbar & tug was connected to the jet & we were towed back to gate. After the checklists were completed I proceeded to do a visual inspection; where I found an approximately 5 foot scrape on the underside of the fuselage; outboard of the right side nose gear door. I made another PA from the L1 door area informing the guests that there would be a tail swap & what our new gate was; then made an AC logbook entry describing the damage I observed. The flight proceeded as normal to ZZZ1 after a 2 hour delay to get everything ready on the jet we swapped into. Not sure if time was a big factor or not. The ramp personnel did not seem rushed but we did push back several minutes after departure time due to the jet being fueled late. Parking an A-321 at [this] gate with the current construction process ongoing may present a challenge to the push back crew due to the longer fuselage & trying to avoid the construction area adjacent to gate. My biggest suggestion would be for the push back crew to communicate any difficulty they may be having with any ground operation. In this circumstance we could have easily stopped the jet; set the parking brakes; & requested a taxi from our current position. We strive to comply with directions given; however; sometimes we need to ask to amend those instructions to meet the current situation.

column121: Beginning the descent into ZZZ at 38;000 ft.; 'open descent' was selected. As the power came back to approaching idle there was a thump; followed by another louder thump. The master caution alerted and an ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor) displayed showing ENG 2 STALL. As soon as we began to apply the procedure; the ECAM cleared itself. No other abnormal engine indications were noted.
column123: Approaching ZZZ; Center had us at 38;000 ft. and slightly past our top of descent. When cleared lower with the autopilot and auto thrust engaged; I selected 'open descent' to start down. Almost immediately; as the thrust was coming back to idle; I heard a muffled sound that was unusual; and felt a small movement of the aircraft; similar to a jet bridge lightly bumping the airplane. As I was processing in my mind what it was; it happened again; accompanied by a master caution light and an ENG 2 STALL on the ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor). Right after I saw the ECAM; it went away. Now the engines were stable at idle; and all engine instruments looked normal. Shortly thereafter; we received an ACARS Maintenance message; confirming what we saw. We turned on engine anti-ice for descent though clouds; and discussed what we saw; felt and heard. We continued into ZZZ and discussed considerations in case the engine stalled again; but really thought it was a transient; isolated event. We didn't experience any further abnormalities the rest of the way in; and wrote up the event upon arrival and called Maintenance to inform them. After following up with Maintenance the next day; I learned they had found damage in the high pressure compressor section of the #2 engine.We had no indications; before or after; of any engine issues. I think there was an AML entry a few days earlier concerning the #2 engine; but it seems to me; it was a reverser issue. Since we were kept high; we were in an idle descent until we were on final approach. It was less than 25 minutes from the compressor stall until landing. I'm curious about the damage. Was it a result of the stall or possibly pre-existing which resulted in the compressor stall?I do not think you can prevent events like this from happening 100 percent of the time. These GE engines are normally very reliable; and if the damage occurred prior to or immediately after the stall; I am even more impressed with them. We didn't notice any abnormal indications or vibrations; outside of the two stalls within a few seconds of each other.

column121: I fell victim to the dirty dozen; complacency. I was reading the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) to perform the leak test of the P1 and pitot S1 system when; in the middle of the test; I realized the airspeed indicator was not indicating correctly. I went back through the manual to realize that I had read it incorrectly. I saw that the circuit breakers needed to be 'opened' instead of 'closed;' which conflicted with what I thought I read. When I inspected the left and right pitot probes I saw the inner sleeve of our test equipment had melted around it and entered the probes; which caused the erroneous readings. After removing the damaged sleeves I realized that the test equipment; DPS1000; had a maximum limit of 60 HZ and should not have been plugged in to the aircraft galley outlet;which exceeds that limit. I did not see the limit on the test device due to it being on when I plugged it in. It booted up and tested normally so I did not look at that part of the device. I detected the problem by realizing the airspeed indication was not lining up correctly with the test equipment.It was my first time doing any work on pitot probes so I wanted to move slowly and read the manual; after being on the task for 6 hours and at the final stretch to finish it I began to lose focus. After I found the problem I began talking to my partner about writing a report and doing damage control by removing the damaged equipment.When I was looking through the manual my eyes went right to the breakers; glossing over the warnings and cautions. Maybe having those color coded; since we no longer have to print out papers due to the electronic systems in place; would be beneficial and more eye catching.

column121: I was conducting a Part 135.293 flight evaluation. The flight had progressed smoothly for approximately 2 hours and we had already flown all required maneuvers as well as two instrument approaches. We were just about finished with the practice approach for the VOR-A circle to land. We had descended to our circling minimums of 980 ft. as we began the circle to the east for a right downwind. [We were] visual at this point at about 100 kts. and flaps set to 'Approach' when he initiated his base-to-final turn. It was evident that he was going to overshoot the runway and I asked him what he thought to which he did not immediately verbally answer but in turn steepened the bank to try and make it. It was at this point that I announced 'Go-Around' and [Pilot Flying] aggressively pushed the power lever forward without immediately pulling the airplane out of its descending turn. It became evident that I had to take controls and as I was pulling back on the yoke and leveling the aircraft the power had already risen to 2615 torque which I immediately and aggressively pulled back to compensate. We completed the positive exchange of controls as we were climbing out to the west of the tower up to the pattern altitude of about 1500 ft. Keep in mind; all of this happened in a mere 2-3 second time period between us both realizing the unstable turn and the go-around maneuver. Upon re-establishing the aircraft and configuring it for the next approach; the yellow 'ETM EXCEED' annunciation popped up in the panel. I knew that the annunciator had something to do with the engine briefly being outside of its rated limits; but my training and experience has taught me that if the engine is in fact in an over torqued state; a red 'TORQUE EXCEED' annunciator comes on and immediate landing is required. With it only being the 'ETM EXCEED' light being Engine Trend Monitor light; I conducted the rest of the flight as usual. We re-flew the circle to land maneuver; which he excelled at on the second try and went about the rest of the Check Ride (touch and go's and one final practice ILS). As the Pilot Monitoring (PM) and Check Airman; it was my duty and responsibility to keep an eye on all factors going on at all times. It was a VMC day with a lot of traffic (two other aircraft in the pattern); I was monitoring the airspeed and aircraft attitude; the very actions and explanations and engine instruments along with an electrical issue that maintenance had made me aware of prior that day. My work load was extremely high that morning; but I noticed the addition of too much power within mere fractions of a second and the torque gauge had not stabilized to a specific setting yet when I already reacted to counter the situation. The First Officer training consists of one week theory training in a classroom setting and one three hour flight which may be extended to another three hour flight if training records indicate. The pilot was explained to me as a good pilot whom did well during his training in both ground class as well as inflight. Up to the incident; nothing that pilot did indicated to me that there was a major discrepancy on theoretical knowledge of the procedures and the only shortcoming was the lack of time spent in aircraft. His flight training was conducted in one of our Legacy 208B aircraft and the check ride was conducted in the newer and glass panel avionics suite-equipped EX aircraft which has drastically different gauges and system knowledge requirements. The pilot had never flown such an aircraft before and there was some general coaching going on about the various digital indications and procedures and I did tell him during the first take off briefing that the digital torque gauge in the EX display panel has a major and very noticeable lag to it and he should set the takeoff power using the analog torque gauge which sits low and very out of sight on the instrument panel of the aircraft. However; pilot had already successfully flown two previous missed approaches with proper torque setting and call outs for the takeoff power to be set by the pilot monitoring. He had also recovered from two different stall maneuvers earlier in the evaluation; both with no major deficiencies. He acted as a professional and knowledgeable pilot up until the incident where he panicked and rushed the power forward more so than he should have. My reaction was to take control of the aircraft and correct the excessive torque setting back to a more appropriate setting for the flight condition at hand. [I suggest to] add more thorough training on take-off procedures and go-around procedures. Especially on the roles of Pilot Flying as well as Pilot Monitoring. Many new hire applicants for the First Officer role have no experience with this and it is in their old habit to do all of the power changes and flap setting adjustments. It is crucial that they do not ever just jam the power lever full forward without asking for the proper take off power to be set.

column121: I listened to the AWOS and noted wind at 5mph from 90 degrees with gusting to 10mph. On final approach for landing; I experienced light to moderate wind gusts that bounced the aircraft around a bit. Under those conditions; I decided to limit flaps to 20 degrees and maintain a slightly higher airspeed since the runway length was over 6;000 ft. and gusting was intermittent. Upon crossing over the runway threshold at 65kts; I reduced power to idle and flared 10 feet over the runway. The aircraft floated in the ground effect for a long distance and ultimately when the wheels made contact it bounced up into the air again and floated further in ground effect. At that moment; a wind gust pushed the tail to the left. I tried to correct with opposite rudder but the deflection did not correct the alignment before the wheels made contact with the runway. The aircraft was by then oriented at a 25-30 degree angle to the right of runway centerline. The aircraft then bolted violently to the right and rolled quickly off the runway into the grass; heading toward a rock lined; 4-ft deep drainage ditch just beyond a taxiway. As I attempted to maneuver the rolling aircraft back to the left; it began to skid and tip over to the right. I righted the aircraft to avoid driving the right wing and nose into the ground and potentially flipping the aircraft; but by then my only choice was to either roll toward the ditch or in the direction of hangars to the right. I braked but wasn't able to stop before the aircraft rolled into the ditch.The left wingtip; propeller and landing gear received damage. No injuries to myself or damage to airport property resulted. I immediately contacted the aircraft owner and airport authorities; who arrived to the scene quickly to assess the situation. The airport manager confirmed no damage to airport property. The aircraft owner and airport manager coordinated to make arrangements to remove the aircraft from the ditch.

column121: Climbing out; approximately XX00Z; the left engine had loss of thrust associated with compressor stall / surges. In the descent we completed the appropriate checklists; acquired the [weight and balance] data for landing in addition to brake cooling then were vectored for a visual approach to [Runway] XXL. We landed uneventfully and taxied clear of the runway and we were met by Fire and Rescue. We shut down the #1 engine and awaited CFR to evaluate. column123: Normal climbout passing FL 282.  Initially heard banging outside of aircraft followed by a reduction in climb; decreasing airspeed and aircraft vibration.  Immediately followed by a call from the A F/A (flight attendant) reporting flame emanating from #1 engine.  Engine problem was confirmed in the cockpit by high temp (800 EGT) and diminished N1.  My F/O (First Officer) immediately notified ATC that we have an engine issue and need to maintain FL 280. I told him to [request priority] at that time. I reduced the thrust lever to observe changes in engine indications. The vibrations ceased and temperature reduction. We both believed we had a compressor stall. We were holding FL 280 on one engine; albeit with excessive thrust on #2 engine.  F/O asked for lower and we were cleared to FL 240. We had two jumpseaters onboard; so I got an experienced set of eyes on the engine.  He confirmed all that we knew and that the engine no longer had flames coming from the tailpipe. Assessing the non-normal together; I called for the QRC (quick reference checklist) Engine Limit or Surge or Stall Checklist.  The QRH (quick reference handbook) confirmed our assessment. We completed down to Step X (QRH) at that point. An engine shutdown was not required; but thrust lever remained at idle for remainder of flight.  ZZZ was 80 miles from our present position and we agreed was the nearest suitable airport.  ATC cleared us direct. While I was PF (pilot flying); F/O communicated with F/A's and passengers.  I sent a message to Dispatch about our diversion.  We ran the Diversion Checklist.  F/O ran weight and balance data for a 'One Engine Inoperative' approach and landing data.  We planned for and flew a 'One Engine Inoperative Landing'.  An uneventful landing in ZZZ culminated with a check of the engine/damage by Emergency Personnel.  We taxied under our own power to the gate.

Once they stated that they saw no visible damage we taxied to gate. The Captain handled flying the aircraft as well as talking to the flight attendants/passengers during this [situation] and I was handling the QRH. Once I was done with the checklists; I took over the radios while returning to ZZZ. We returned single engine with a flaps 20 landing. I quickly realized the aircraft began to move forward. My seatbelt and the max-back seat position made it impossible for me to reach both brake/rudder pedals and stop the aircraft. My lesson is to reset the brakes pressing hard on the brake pedals once I get back inside the plane.  I'll also avoid any seat adjustment after engine start-up. column121: We were taxing for departure. As the aircraft got closer it became readily apparent that the aircraft was lined up with the taxiway on which we were parked and was going to pass dangerously close if it continued on its current trajectory. Fearing a collision I advanced the power levers; simultaneously released the parking brake and [as] the aircraft moved forward the left main gear exited the tarmac and the left prop struck an elevated reflector. The Citation passed overhead over the aft portion of the aircraft at what I estimated to be approximately 20-25 ft. above our aircraft and appeared to be initiating a go around. I heard the Citation pilot call 'Going around' and admonishing us for being on the runway at which point first [the F/O] and myself corrected him by telling him he had just overflown us on the taxiway he then apologized saying something about no runway lights. I taxied the aircraft to parking shut down; called Maintenance. A combination of inoperative runway edge lighting; the Citation pilot's decision to continue approach and attempt to land with inadequate lighting and failure to execute a go-around until prompted on the CTAF frequency. The damage to [our aircraft] was the direct result of rapid evasive maneuvering to avoid a possible collision with the Citation attempting to land on the taxiway.
